en.title: Are AI Overviews Taking Your Search Traffic?
en.titleCore: Are AI Overviews Taking Your Search Traffic? What the Click Data Shows
en.description: Pew and Ahrefs find fewer clicks in studied AI Overview conditions. Learn what their data proves, what it cannot, and how to diagnose your own search traffic.
en.body:
Yes, AI Overviews can reduce clicks from some search-result pages, but the evidence does not show that they caused every site's recent traffic drop. Pew observed fewer traditional-result clicks when an AI summary appeared; Ahrefs estimated a lower position-one click-through rate for AI Overview queries. Neither result diagnoses an individual site's October 2026 decline.

That distinction matters when a search report suddenly looks alarming. Google's October 16–19 ranking-volatility discussion was community reporting, not confirmation of a new Google rollout. Separately, Google announced interface changes to AI Mode and AI Overviews on October 15, including more prominent inline links and broader article carousels. Those changes could affect click behavior, but Google did not connect them to the reported volatility or any particular site's traffic. Search Engine Roundtable, updated October 19; Google, October 15.

What evidence says AI Overviews may take clicks?

Pew Research Center analyzed browser activity from 900 U.S. adults during March 2025 and reconstructed the Google results for 68,879 searches. In that observational dataset, people clicked a traditional result on 8% of visits to pages with an AI summary, compared with 15% when no summary appeared. A click on a cited link inside the summary occurred on 1% of visits to pages with a summary. These percentages describe observed next actions, not a randomized experiment or a forecast for every query.

The finding supports a plausible mechanism: when a result page answers more of a query before a person visits a site, some clicks may not happen. It does not tell a publisher how many clicks it would have received for its own queries without an AI summary, and it does not show that AI summaries explain all organic-search decline.

How large might the click-through effect be?

Ahrefs' February 2026 update examined aggregated desktop Search Console data for 300,000 keywords: 150,000 that triggered an AI Overview in December 2025 and 150,000 informational keywords without one. It compared December 2023 and December 2025 CTR, then used the non-AI-Overview group to estimate a counterfactual for the AI Overview group. Ahrefs reported 1.6% actual position-one CTR for the latter group against a modeled 3.7% without the Overview, describing the gap as about 58% lower.

The studies point in the same direction, but measure different things. Pew reports observed user actions on result pages; Ahrefs estimates a position-one CTR difference across keyword groups and time. Neither should be translated directly into “our website lost this share of traffic.” Clicks also depend on impressions and CTR: fewer impressions, lower CTR, or both can reduce clicks.

Did AI Overviews cause the October 2026 traffic reports?

The available public evidence does not establish that. Google's Search Status Dashboard shows the September 2026 spam update ended October 8, and it lists no October 15–19 ranking incident. Search Engine Roundtable's October 16 report and October 19 update describe community chatter, not a confirmed rollout. Google separately announced October 15 changes to AI Mode and AI Overviews: more prominent inline links, a test of a dedicated official-sites section, and wider availability of timely-article carousels. Google did not say those interface updates caused the reported volatility or explain any site's traffic movement. Google Search Status Dashboard.

For a specific site, ask whether the loss is mostly fewer impressions, weaker CTR on comparable queries, or a shift in query and page mix. Search Console includes AI Overview and AI Mode links in overall web-search performance, rather than giving publishers a direct, complete causal counterfactual. Compare matched query-page groups over time, check dates and devices, and annotate product-interface changes. Treat the result as diagnosis, not proof of cause.

How should a team measure and budget for the change?

Keep three quantities separate: search exposure (impressions and position), visits (clicks and analytics sessions), and business value (qualified leads or revenue). For each important query-page group, calculate CTR as clicks divided by impressions and compare like-for-like periods. Then check whether qualified outcomes changed, accounting for conversion lag. A citation or AI visibility count is an exposure signal; it is not automatically a visit or a return on content spend.

Do not pause or expand AI content budgets based on a short traffic dip alone. First identify whether the affected query set shows lower CTR with stable impressions, reduced visibility, or a mix. Set a review window that matches the conversion cycle, test changes on a bounded group where possible, and record both costs and outcomes. Pew and Ahrefs offer evidence that click displacement is plausible at the search-result level; only a site's own query-level evidence can show how much it matters there.

What else should publishers know?

Are AI Overviews taking clicks away from websites? Research from Pew and Ahrefs finds fewer or lower click-through rates in studied conditions, but the methods differ and neither provides a universal site-level loss rate.

Does a 58% CTR decline mean my site lost 58% of traffic? No. Ahrefs' 58% compares observed position-one CTR with its modeled counterfactual for one keyword cohort. It is not total traffic loss.

Can the October 2026 Google volatility be blamed on AI Overviews? The cited evidence does not establish that. Community chatter is not a confirmed update, and Google's October 15 AI interface announcement does not attribute ranking or site traffic changes to those features.

What should I check first? Compare clicks, impressions, CTR, and average position for matched query-page groups, then inspect analytics sessions and qualified outcomes separately.

Which sources support this analysis?

Research checked October 19, 2026. Read Pew's study and methodology, Ahrefs' methods and estimates, Google's AI-feature measurement guidance, and the dated volatility report. Recheck live sources before publication.
